instructions: The day before, at least 14 hours ahead: rinse the 1 cup rice and 1/4 tsp fenugreek seeds in a bowl a few times, until the water runs mostly clear. Cover them with plenty of fresh water and leave them to soak for at least 4 hours.
At the same time, rinse 1/3 cup of the urad dal, the 2 tsp toor dal and 2 tsp of the chana dal in a second bowl. Cover them with fresh water and leave them to soak for at least 2 hours.

Drain the dals well and put them in a blender with 1/2 cup water. Blend for 4 to 5 minutes, stopping to scrape down the sides, until the batter is smooth, pale and fluffy. Add up to 2 tbsp more water if the blades stall. Give the blender a short break if the jar gets warm. Transfer the batter into a large bowl.

Rinse the 1/3 cup poha and drain it. Drain the rice and put it in the blender with the poha and 1/3 cup water. Blend until it feels like fine semolina when you rub a little between your fingers. Add it to the dal batter and mix them together well with your hand.
Cover the bowl and leave it somewhere warm overnight, 8 to 12 hours, until the batter has about doubled and looks bubbly. If your kitchen is cold, set it in the oven with only the light on.

In the morning, put the 3 potatoes in a pot, cover them with cold water and bring it to a boil over high. Turn it down and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, until a knife slides in easily but they're not falling apart.
Meanwhile, thinly slice the onion. Seed and finely chop the green chili, finely chop the ginger, and chop 2 tbsp of the cilantro. Squeeze the lemon. That should be about 2 tbsp of juice.
Drain the potatoes and peel them once you can handle them. Crumble them into rough chunks.

Heat 2 tbsp of the oil in a large frying pan over medium. Add the 1 tsp mustard seeds. When they start to pop, after about 30 seconds, add the remaining 1 tsp urad dal, the remaining 1 tsp chana dal, the dried red chili, the curry leaves from 1 sprig and the pinch of hing. Stir for about 1 minute, until the dals turn golden. Stand back a little. The leaves spatter.
Add the chili and ginger and stir for 30 seconds. Add the onion and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring now and then, until it's soft and has shrunk a little.
Stir in the 1/4 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp of the salt. Add the potatoes and 2 tbsp water, and mash them lightly with the spoon as you mix. Cook for 2 minutes, until it's all yellow and hot through.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the cilantro and the lemon juice. Taste it, and add a pinch more salt if it's flat. Set it aside.
Stir the remaining 3/4 tsp salt gently into the batter. It should pour slowly off a ladle in a thick ribbon. If it's thicker than that, stir in water a spoonful at a time.
Heat a large cast iron pan, nonstick pan or tawa over medium high. Rub it with a few drops of the remaining oil on a paper towel. It's ready when a few drops of water sizzle away at once.
Pour about 1/3 cup batter into the middle of the pan. Straight away, spread it outward in a spiral with the back of the ladle, pressing lightly, until it's a thin round about 9 inches across.
Dot about 1 tsp of the butter over the dosa and around the edge. Cook it for 2 to 3 minutes, until the underside is golden and crisp and the edge lifts from the pan.
Spoon about 1/3 cup of the potato filling down the middle. Fold both sides over it, or roll it up, and slide it onto a plate.
Make the rest the same way. Wipe the pan with a drop of oil each time, and let it get hot again before you pour. You'll get about 9.
Serve hot with coconut chutney and sambar.
advance_prep_notes: Soak the rice and dals at least 4 hours, then grind the batter and ferment it overnight, the day before.
method_notes: Both versions soak rice with fenugreek seeds and the dals separately, grind the dal smooth and fluffy and the rice a little coarse with poha, ferment the batter overnight, and fill each crisp, buttered dosa with a potato bhaji tempered with mustard seeds, curry leaves and hing. Hebbar's Kitchen adds toor dal to the batter, salts it only after fermenting, and finishes the potatoes with cilantro and lemon juice. Swasthi's soaks the dals for 4 to 5 hours, uses a little less urad dal, cooks the onions until lightly golden and skips the lemon. This follows Hebbar's at a third of the amount, for about 9 dosas, with one seeded chili so the filling stays mild.
